body_text: There’s a mystery afoot in the tony Chicago neighborhood of Lincoln Park. Someone appears to be paying workers to spread nuts and seeds across the eponymous green space. The workers wear matching latex gloves and tote identical green bags filled with feed, the Wall Street Journal reports . Their employer appears to be an animal-loving local eccentric who just so happens to be a billionaire: Barbara Seid, whose husband Barre is the reclusive former owner of Tripp Lite, an electrical equipment maker. Her aim, it seems, is to attract and feed squirrels, who she adores. Her neighbors and city regulators don't agree. Feeding animals subjects offenders to a civil ticket and fine. That’s not much of a deterrent for a billionaire and neighbors and city officials are exploring other ways to crackdown on the arboreal banquet, which has somewhat predictably attracted rats who are now burrowing in the park. Stocks surged on Monday after Nvidia ’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. The chipmaker’s shares skyrocketed, ending the day up 31%, and pulling big chunks of the AI trade and broad indices up with it. (More on that absolutely massive story below.) In one of the most shocking corporate announcements in years, Nvidia said Monday that it was reinstalling former CEO Jensen Huang at the helm of the company, reversing the decision which the same body had taken less than two weeks ago. Nvidia shares immediately surged, boosting the large swathes of the flagging AI trade, the S&P 500, and the Nasdaq 100. How exactly did this happen? After all, it was only November 12 when Huang resigned under pressure as news broke that he’d had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who is the CEO of a massive Nvidia customer that was suspected of smuggling chips to China, along with a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee. Well, in its announcement of Huang’s stunning reinstatement, Nvidia’s board said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. It’s now fairly clear exactly how senior those US government officials are. The New York Times reports that President Trump and Vice President Vance were intimately involved in Huang’s restoration. "Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation, the NYT reports . “Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed." Trump was so deeply involved in Huang’s reinstatement that he dialed into the board’s meeting to argue for the return of the previously defenestrated executive, Semafor reported . In a call-in interview with CNBC, President Trump expressed fear that if Nvidia did not re-hire Huang, he could defect, effectively seeking corporate asylum from the Chinese. “Jensen could take the next plane to China,” Trump said , “and I can guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted… And then they would automatically have all of the thing.” The president said on CNBC that in terms of national security risk, he told the board, “we believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine. I gave them [the board] enough assurance.” The upshot is that 12 days after he resigned as CEO over affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and a subordinate, seven days since the company’s CFO and interim CEO presided over releasing better-than-expected earnings results, and six days since the board reportedly made contact with the CEO of a competitor to discuss the Nvidia CEO job, Huang is back in charge of Nvidia. If all of this seems a little chaotic from the outside, take some solace that it appears to be just as chaotic on the inside: Bloomberg reports that interim CEO Collette Kress and other senior management at Nvidia were not consulted about the move by the board, and were only informed of the shocking reversal at the last minute. Nvidia shares ended the day up almost a third, adding just shy of a whopping $1 trillion in market value. Nvidia shareholders, who had recently suffered a painful bout of key man risk, are now getting their key man reward. And in case you were concerned, FT Alphaville pointed out that in the final paragraph of the press release announcing Huang’s return, Nvidia noted it is “commencing a search to fill a new position” that will report directly to a board committee: “Chief Compliance Officer.” Regardless of what new internal policies and procedures Nvidia puts in place, this saga is far from over. Huang was already scheduled to provide behind-closed-doors Senate testimony on December 3. That Capitol Hill appearance has now been upgraded to a public hearing, ensuring several hours of blockbuster live TV coverage. Of course, the tenor in Washington, DC is about to shift dramatically in January when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And if Democrats are looking for any materials to subpoena, there’s always the results and work product of that independent review of Huang that Nvidia’s board initiated a mere three weeks ago. The nature of the end has been a matter of consideration for time immemorial, from the psychedelic if symbolic visions of the revelation of John, the fantasies of atomic annihilation of the Cold War to the realities of kinetic destruction of the Cretaceous. How does the apocalypse proceed? Is it a sharp destruction, such as the Fall of Troy, or a gradual and barely imperceptible decline in state capacity, such as the Fall of Rome? I speak, of course, of the SaaSpocalypse. The foretold doom of the software business, hastened along by the rise of AI. This past and these next two weeks, we see earnings from a number of big names in the once-booming software-as-a-service industry who once feared the fiery doom of a swift AI-driven demise but have survived that; Salesforce seem like they’re going to ride this thing out. But don’t let that deceive you. Just because the margins of the SaaS companies have not been atomized by arsenals of agents doesn’t mean that a slow-moving apocalypse isn’t in motion in some areas. Indeed, it has been going on for quite some time. The name of the fourth horseman of this SaaSPocalypse is not ChatGPT Codex, though. It’s Bending Spoons , which released earnings last Thursday and announced a new acquisition that advances its mission of rolling up the detritus of the SaaS boom into a viable firm. You may not know Bending Spoons off the dome, but you know (and may very well use!) their products. The company went public over the summer and has set out to buy up companies that once had sky-high valuations but have since abruptly returned to reality. The classic format of a Bending Spoons headline is something like “[ Somewhat recognizable app ]-owner Bending Spoons purchases [ slightly more well-known app ].” You have seen this headline a dozen times. In fact, you can build a pretty reliable timeline of the company by daisy-chaining headlines in this exact format: July, 2024: Italy’s Bending Spoons Buys WeTransfer September, 2025 : WeTransfer owner Bending Spoons buys Vimeo December, 2025 : Vimeo owner Bending Spoons buys AOL July, 2026 : AOL Owner Bending Spoons jumps 40% after IPO August, 2026 : Newly public Bending Spoons buys AirTable Their modus operandi is to buy up mature companies that have maximized their total addressable market at a fraction of their once-high valuations, and then put these relatively boring businesses under the control of small, well-paid teams to manage them . Crucially, Bending Spoons employees run the apps they own, with previous staff usually let go in large-scale layoffs pretty quickly after the acquisition. And it’s not just layoffs, either. Bending Spoons relies on price hikes too. So, lower overhead, higher revenue, a decently-locked in user base, you get the ideal. Berkshire Hathaway , the investment firm that built an empire by investing in boring companies like utilities and insurance companies that had unsexy businesses that spun off cash predictably, has acquired a 10% stake in the company. Last week, they struck again, buying Mailchimp from Intuit for $3.68 billion, which is a third of the price paid by Intuit in 2021. While the various AI-driven news cycles have rattled the valuations of the SaaS giants, they seem fine, right? Saaspocalypse averted? Not quite, and this week will be revealing. Just because the Saaspocalypse doesn’t look like the overnight collapse of an empire doesn’t mean it’s not happening. Lots of these companies are trading at a fraction of their valuation and an even smaller fraction of their aspirations. Heck, this week we’ll get an update from Zoom , which is trucking along at a $24.5 billion market cap, not meaningfully different from where they were trading in 2019 before the pandemic that propelled them, at one point, north of a $140 billion market valuation. They say that the standard civilian experience of the fall of the Roman empire was when your local bridge went out and nobody came around to fix it. body_text: A slew of states have now enacted cell phone bans in schools, which keep phones, watches and connected tablets locked away from bell-to-bell. Some of the immediate benefits, like encouraging students to, uhhh, talk to each other, are obvious. Harvard researchers, however, took things a step further. They looked at students in 4,600 schools across the US and found that school cell phone bans helped students learn more. They found that in schools where phones and other devices were kept locked away during the day, students gained the academic equivalent of one to two additional weeks of instruction per year, the Wall Street Journal reported . “Pretty soon we’ll look back and think it’s crazy that students could use their phones whenever they want to,” Thomas Kane, an author of the study and director of the Harvard Center for Education Policy Research, told the WSJ. Earlier this week I wrote that American consumers feeling increasingly pessimistic about the cost of living was increasingly not Walmart ’s problem. Case in point: The retail giant reported earnings results that narrowly beat Wall Street estimates and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. Its US e-commerce sales jumped 23%, even as comparable sales growth slowed from a year earlier. Target , another place that sells both staples and cheap knickknacks, crushed quarterly estimates and hiked its guidance after posting its best sales growth in five years. TJX , which owns discount retailers TJ Maxx and Marshalls, also beat estimates. These retailers describe catering to a value-conscious customer. “Busy families are watching their budgets and being thoughtful about where they spend, and we see them responding when we give them something they love at a price that feels right,” Cara Sylvester, chief merchandising officer at Target, told analysts. US retail sales slowed in October as purchases of big-ticket items like cars and furniture slipped, according to the most recent reading from the Commerce Department released Tuesday. That checks out with what both Home Depot and Lowe’s reported: smaller repair and maintenance projects helped drive their sales beats, even as larger discretionary renovations remained under pressure. Both face macroeconomic headwinds, like high borrowing costs and a slow housing market. “Well, Simeon, housing turnover hasn't moved in four years now,” Richard McPhail, Home Depot’s current CFO and incoming CEO, quipped at a Morgan Stanley analyst. He attributed several positive quarters to market share gains. “Our investments are designed to position us to capture share regardless of the economic environment,” he said. Retailers seem to be successfully adapting to a world where people are pinching pennies and feel like life is ripping them off. Target is cutting prices, TJ Maxx is trying to attract bargain hunters across income brackets, and Home Depot is catering to homeowners who would rather fix up their current place than trade their cheap mortgage for a much more expensive one. The industry appears to be well poised for a strong holiday shopping season. For now, retailers seem to have figured out how to keep Americans spending even when they don't feel particularly good about it.
